Esports. Competitive video gaming organized at professional, televised, and international scales. Emerging from arcade tournaments and LAN parties in the nineteen nineties, esports evolved from underground subculture into a billion-dollar industry with franchised teams, stadium events, and global audiences. The legitimacy and infrastructure of esports now rivals traditional sports in organizational sophistication while retaining gaming's accessibility and digital-native communities.

Origins trace to early nineteen eighties arcade competitions with Donkey Kong and Pac-Man, but modern esports infrastructure crystallized with StarCraft in South Korea during the early two thousands, where pro gamers became televised celebrities.

Counter-Strike became foundational to Western esports legitimacy. Its tactical depth, accessibility, and competitive purity made it the first game to sustain a truly global pro circuit across decades.

The Multiplayer Online Battle Arena genre—particularly League of Legends and Dota Two—scaled esports into stadiums. The annual League of Legends World Championship rivals traditional sports events in viewership and prize pools.

Esports adopted the franchise model borrowed from traditional sports, replacing open-circuit tournaments. Teams like T1, Fnatic, and Team Liquid command sponsorship, salaries, and broadcast rights rivaling major sports leagues.

Twitch, founded in twenty eleven, and YouTube Gaming transformed esports infrastructure by making live viewership and community interaction central to the medium itself, not ancillary to competition.

Prize pools have grown exponentially. Dota Two's International offering thirty million dollars or more annually and Fortnite tournaments demonstrate esports' capacity to attract venture-scale investment and mainstream corporate sponsorship.

Youth participation and skill ceiling remain esports' defining feature. Unlike traditional sports, reaction time and mechanical precision peak in the late teens and early twenties, creating shorter professional careers but lower barriers to entry.
